subject: english-language
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the Individual Task in Component 4?
options: A prepared talk or presentation on a topic chosen by the candidate
A written essay handed to the examiner
A silent reading exercise
A grammar test on Standard English
questions.explain: The Individual Task requires the candidate to deliver a prepared talk on a topic of their own choice.

questions.q: Approximately how long should the Individual Task talk last?
options: 3 to 4 minutes
30 seconds
15 minutes
1 hour
questions.explain: The individual talk is designed to last roughly three to four minutes.

questions.q: Who chooses the topic for the Individual Task?
options: The candidate
The exam board, which sets one topic for everyone
Another student in the class
The moderator on the day at random
questions.explain: Candidates select their own topic so they can speak with knowledge and interest.

questions.q: Why is it an advantage to choose a topic the candidate knows well?
options: It allows sustained, detailed and engaging talk
It guarantees full marks automatically
It removes the need to use Standard English
It means the discussion can be skipped
questions.explain: Genuine knowledge lets a candidate sustain and develop their ideas convincingly.

questions.q: A candidate reads their talk word-for-word from a full script in a flat monotone. What would most improve their delivery?
options: Use brief prompt notes and vary tone and pace to engage the listener
Read the same script faster to finish sooner
Add long silent pauses throughout
Recite the whole script from memory even more quickly
questions.explain: Speaking from prompts with vocal variety communicates far more effectively than reading aloud.

questions.q: Why should the talk have a clear opening, development and conclusion?
options: It helps the listener follow the ideas in a logical, cohesive order
It is required to be exactly one hundred words
It replaces the need for a discussion afterwards
It avoids the use of Standard English
questions.explain: A clear structure lets ideas be presented in a coherent, sustained sequence.

questions.q: What normally follows the Individual Task in the test?
options: A discussion developing the topic with the examiner
A written examination
A group debate with other candidates
A reading-comprehension paper
questions.explain: The talk is followed by a discussion in which the examiner develops the same topic.

questions.q: What is the main aim of the Discussion?
options: To develop and explore the ideas of the individual task in more depth
To test the candidate's spelling
To have the candidate read a passage aloud
To have the candidate repeat the talk word for word
questions.explain: The discussion extends and deepens the ideas raised in the individual task.

questions.q: During the discussion, what should the candidate mainly do?
options: Respond thoughtfully to the examiner's questions and develop their points
Stay silent and let the examiner talk
Change to a completely different topic
Ask the examiner to answer instead
questions.explain: Candidates are assessed on how well they engage with and extend the discussion.

questions.q: The examiner asks, 'Can you explain why you think that?' What is the best response?
options: Give clear reasons and examples to develop the point
Simply answer 'yes'
Change the subject
Repeat the examiner's question back
questions.explain: Supporting a view with reasons and examples shows the ability to sustain and develop talk.

questions.q: Why do repeated one-word answers limit a candidate's marks in the discussion?
options: They show little ability to sustain and develop talk
They use too much Standard English
They make the discussion too long
They break an examination rule
questions.explain: Minimal answers give no evidence of the extended, developed talk the discussion rewards.

questions.q: A candidate disagrees with a point the examiner makes. What is the most effective approach?
options: Explain their own view politely with supporting reasons
Refuse to answer the question
Immediately agree without thinking
Talk over the examiner to make the point
questions.explain: Politely justifying a differing view demonstrates confident, developed spoken engagement.

questions.q: Effective conversation and discussion require the candidate to do what?
options: Listen carefully and respond appropriately
Ignore what the other speaker says
Speak only in memorised sentences
Avoid all eye contact
questions.explain: This component assesses listening and responding as well as speaking.

questions.q: Why is listening as important as speaking in this component?
options: Responses must connect to what has been said, showing genuine engagement
Listening earns no marks at all
It simply gives the candidate a rest
It is only ever tested in the written papers
questions.explain: Good listening allows replies that build directly on the examiner's contributions.

questions.q: In this formal spoken assessment, candidates are expected to use what?
options: Spoken Standard English in an appropriate register
Only regional slang
Text-message abbreviations
Long stretches of silence
questions.explain: Formal speaking tasks reward clear use of spoken Standard English in a suitable register.

questions.q: What does 'adapting register to the situation' mean?
options: Adjusting formality and vocabulary to suit the audience and purpose
Speaking as loudly as possible at all times
Using exactly the same tone in every situation
Reading everything from a written script
questions.explain: Register is the level of formality and word choice adapted to context and listener.

questions.q: Speaking to the examiner in a formal test, a candidate is tempted to use casual slang. What is the better choice?
options: Use clear, appropriately formal Standard English
Use text-message abbreviations
Mumble to appear relaxed
Use as much slang as possible
questions.explain: A formal assessment calls for clear Standard English rather than casual slang.

questions.q: How do non-verbal features such as eye contact and appropriate pace help a speaker?
options: They aid clear communication and help engage the listener
They remove the need to speak at all
They are automatically penalised
They matter only in the written paper
questions.explain: Eye contact, pace and expression support clear, engaging spoken communication.

questions.q: What does Component 4 (Speaking and Listening) chiefly assess?
options: The ability to communicate effectively through speaking and listening
The ability to analyse unseen poetry in writing
The ability to translate texts into English
The ability to read silently at speed
questions.explain: The component tests spoken communication and listening rather than reading or writing.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE First Language English (0500) syllabus; Component 4: Speaking and Listening
